definition: Wishing or intending harm to other people.
example: She mistook his blunt advice for malevolent intent, though he only wanted her to succeed.
nuance: Malevolent stresses a deep-seated wish for harm, while malicious more often describes a particular spiteful act.
prompt: A student learns that a classmate deliberately deleted her group's shared project file.
options: The malevolent classmate erased the file so the group would miss its deadline.
The malevolent classmate stayed late to help the group rebuild every lost page.
The malevolent classmate erased the file by accident while trying to save a copy.
The malevolent classmate complained loudly that the project topic was dull.
reasons: Destroying work on purpose to make others fail shows a clear desire to hurt them.
Pitching in to repair the damage shows goodwill, the reverse of ill intent.
An honest mistake involves no wish to cause harm, so the word does not fit.
Grumbling about a topic shows dissatisfaction, not a desire to injure anyone.

practice.prompt: Readers discuss a scheming uncle in a mystery novel who wants the family fortune.
options: The malevolent uncle quietly paid his niece's college tuition and asked for no thanks.
The malevolent uncle changed his opinions to match whoever had spoken last.
The malevolent uncle was famous at family dinners for his long and terrible puns.
The malevolent uncle forged letters to turn the siblings against each other.
reasons: Generous, selfless giving reflects kindness, which is the opposite quality.
Being easily swayed describes a weak will, not a wish to do others harm.
Corny jokes may annoy people, but they show no intention to hurt anyone.
Deliberately stirring up conflict among relatives for gain reveals real ill will.
